case_study_insert.main_stem: Brightroute Delivery Co-operative (BRD) is a workers' cooperative in the last-mile urban delivery sector, employing a workforce of 40. Founded in 2015 by Tunde Okafor and member couriers, the business delivers parcels for e-commerce retailers across the city using a flat structure with democratic leadership, where member couriers vote on major decisions. BRD plans to invest $520,000 in 25 electric cargo vans for its city-centre routes, financed by a $320,000 bank loan and a $200,000 member share issue. It has fixed costs of $184,000 a year, a variable cost of $4.60 a unit and a selling price of $9.20, and produces 58,000 units a year (each unit being one parcel delivered). BRD faces labour turnover of 31% among its couriers.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Market Research Summary — September 2026: BRD delivered 9,800 parcels last month, with 92.5% arriving within next-day windows, down from 95.0% in May. A survey of 420 online shoppers found that 73% prefer delivery firms using electric vehicles, and 66% would pay $1 extra per parcel for same-day evening slots. Social media mentions of BRD grew 38% this quarter. The repeat purchase rate from partner retailers is 84%. Courier absenteeism reached 8% in August. Members voted to trial Sunday delivery shifts.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Brightroute Delivery Co-operative for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 4.75%, increasing borrowing costs for variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.5% from $10.90 to $11.61 per hour from April 2027, lifting courier pay rates. (3) Electricity and charging costs for electric vehicles have risen 11.3% year-on-year, diesel prices rose 8.7%, while e-commerce parcel volumes grew 9.4% over the same period.

questions.question_text: BRD plans to finance its $520,000 electric cargo van expansion partly with a $200,000 member share issue. Explain two advantages for BRD of using a member share issue to fund the expansion instead of the $320,000 bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A member share issue brings in $200,000 of permanent capital with no mandatory repayments and no interest, which matters because BRD already pays interest payable that rose from $15,000 to $21,000 in 2025 and still carries the $320,000 bank loan. In a co-operative, shares bought by members deepen their commitment to the fleet, align the owners with the vans they will drive, and avoid the risk of the bank seizing vehicles if a trading quarter disappoints — protecting the democratic model and the 40 members' livelihoods.

Point 2: Raising shares from members widens the co-op's capital base without diluting external ownership or ceding any say to a lender, so members retain full democratic control of route policy and working conditions as the 25 vans arrive. The issue also signals member confidence to partner retailers, helping win the same-day evening contracts that 66% of shoppers said they would pay $1 extra for, and it leaves the co-op headroom to borrow again later rather than exhausting its credit line on the $520,000 purchase.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to BRD's financing, expansion and cooperative structure.

questions.question_text: BRD is launching its same-day evening delivery service to e-commerce retailers and shoppers. Consider local radio advertising, short social media video ads, or partnerships with eco-focused delivery bloggers. Which should BRD choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Local radio advertising: Local radio is affordable for a co-operative and reaches city-wide commuters during drive time, which suits a same-day evening promise. It could build general awareness of BRD's green, member-owned model. However, radio offers no visual proof of the electric vans, cannot target online shoppers precisely, and rarely converts directly to parcel bookings; for a service whose buyers discover delivery options inside retailer checkouts, analogue reach is a blunt instrument.

Social media video ads: Short videos showing clean electric cargo vans, real couriers and the same-day evening service speak directly to the 66% of shoppers willing to pay $1 extra for evening slots and the 73% who prefer electric-vehicle delivery firms. Social campaigns are cheap, targeted by postcode and age, and measurable through the 38% growth in mentions already visible — ideal for a 40-member co-op with a small marketing budget and a strong story to tell.

Eco-blogger partnerships: Partnering with sustainability bloggers gives credible third-party endorsement of BRD's electric fleet and could deepen trust with eco-conscious shoppers. The limitation is pace and control: blogger calendars are unpredictable, reach is niche and inconsistent, and messaging may drift from BRD's democratic co-op values, so it works best as a supporting tactic rather than the launch engine.

Recommendation: BRD should choose social media video ads, with selective blogger partnerships layered on once momentum builds. Social video targets exactly the shoppers and retailer buyers BRD needs, is affordable on a co-op budget, and is fully measurable against the same-day promise. Local radio is rejected as poorly targeted and unmeasurable for checkout-driven purchases; eco-blogger partnerships alone are rejected as too slow and inconsistent to carry the launch, though they may reinforce the campaign afterwards.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of promotional options with minimal application to BRD.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of at least two options in the context of BRD with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of BRD with a well-justified recommendation explaining why radio and blogger-only approaches are rejected.

questions.question_text: BRD has labour turnover of 31% among couriers and absenteeism reached 8% in August. Explain two benefits for BRD of using job enrichment to reduce labour turnover.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Job enrichment gives couriers more responsibility — such as planning their own drop sequences, handling retailer queries or mentoring new members — which satisfies higher-level motivators like responsibility and recognition rather than pure pay. Enriched roles make the work more meaningful, directly tackling the 31% churn among couriers who currently treat the job as a short-term gig, and raising commitment to the co-op's flat, democratic culture.

Point 2: Couriers with enriched roles see a clearer link between their effort and BRD's success, so service quality and next-day reliability improve, protecting the 92.5% next-day performance that partner retailers judge contracts on when deciding whether to renew. More involved couriers also spot delivery problems earlier, reducing complaints and re-deliveries, and are far cheaper to develop internally than to replace from scratch — cutting recruitment and induction costs sharply while the absenteeism of 8% recorded in August is pushed back down and the co-op keeps its flat, democratic culture intact.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to BRD's turnover, absenteeism and service reliability.

questions.question_text: BRD must cut courier labour turnover of 31% before the 25 vans arrive. Consider introducing a profit-sharing scheme for member couriers, or job rotation between city-centre routes, warehouse sorting and customer service. Which should BRD choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Profit-sharing scheme: Sharing a portion of BRD's surplus with member couriers aligns everyone with co-operative success, rewards effort directly in cash, and fits democratic ownership — members literally share the profit. With operating profit of $174,000 in 2025 (Appendix 2), even a modest scheme links pay to the 84% retailer repeat rate and motivates cost control on fuel and maintenance. Limitations: payouts shrink when profits fall, weakening motivation exactly when times are hardest, and profit-sharing does not fix boring work or physical strain, so it may not dent turnover on its own.

Job rotation: Rotating couriers across route driving, sorting and customer service adds variety, builds multi-skilled members the co-op needs as the same-day evening service scales, and reduces repetitive strain and boredom. Rotation also lets BRD cover Sunday trial shifts democratically without hiring, and gives couriers visibility of the business beyond the van seat. Drawbacks: it does not raise pay, so turnover driven by wage competition stays, and rotation requires training in sorting and customer systems that may overwhelm 40 members.

Decision: BRD should choose job rotation as the primary tool, supported by a modest profit-sharing top-up. Rotation directly cures the boredom-and-strain root causes of 31% turnover and the 8% August absenteeism, strengthens the multi-skill base the 25-van launch needs, and fits democratic self-management. A profit-sharing-only approach is rejected as the main lever because pay alone does not cure exhaustion and leaves BRD exposed if profits dip after the $520,000 investment; a small profit share can still crown the rotation scheme once vans are in service.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two options with limited application to BRD.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both options in the context of BRD.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options in the context of BRD with a well-justified decision covering cost, variety, skills and co-operative ownership.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how BRD's management can use its cost, break-even and delivery data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $9.20 − $4.60 = $4.60. Answer: contribution per unit is $4.60.
Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $184,000 ÷ ($9.20 − $4.60) = $184,000 ÷ $4.60 = 40,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 40,000 units a year.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways BRD's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. BRD can compare the 40,000-unit break-even output with 58,000 actual parcel deliveries, revealing a margin of safety of 18,000 units — security that the $520,000 van expansion is affordable before members commit further capital.
2. Contribution per unit of $4.60 lets the member forum model charging the $1 same-day evening surcharge that 66% of shoppers would accept, checking whether the higher price still covers the $184,000 fixed costs and $320,000 bank loan.
3. Managers can stress-test the 11.3% rise in electricity and charging costs, since a pricier $4.60 variable cost erodes the $4.60 contribution directly, warning the co-op to renegotiate retailer contracts or lift the delivery price first.
4. Managers can benchmark unit cost — fixed cost per unit of $184,000 ÷ 58,000 = $3.17 plus the $4.60 variable cost, giving $7.77 a unit — to target routes with thin margins, set prices for the Sunday trial, and keep the 84% repeat-purchase rate profitable.

questions.model_answer: (i) Contribution per unit = $4.60 | (ii) Break-even output = 40,000 units | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 18,000 units vs 58,000 deliveries; $1 surcharge modelling for the evening service; stress-testing the 11.3% electricity rise; and unit-cost benchmarking at $7.77 to protect retailer margins.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate BRD's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, the profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has BRD's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 35.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 40.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 10.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 12.0%
ROCE 2024 = 12.0%
ROCE 2025 = 14.5%

Detailed workings: 2024 gross profit = $1,200,000 revenue − $780,000 cost of sales = $420,000, giving $420,000 ÷ $1,200,000 = 35.0%; 2025 = ($1,450,000 − $870,000) = $580,000 ÷ $1,450,000 = 40.0%. After operating expenses: 2024 $120,000 ÷ $1,200,000 = 10.0%; 2025 $174,000 ÷ $1,450,000 = 12.0%. Capital efficiency: 2024 $120,000 ÷ $1,000,000 = 12.0%; 2025 $174,000 ÷ $1,200,000 = 14.5%.

Evaluation: Performance has clearly improved, which matters for a member-owned business whose members rely on distributions and job security. The trading margin widened from 35.0% to 40.0% as electric vans cut diesel exposure and the retailer mix improved, and the operating margin rose from 10.0% to 12.0% despite interest payable increasing from $15,000 to $21,000 as the $320,000 bank loan was drawn. Capital efficiency rose from 12.0% to 14.5% even though capital employed grew by $200,000 to $1,200,000, showing the vans and sorting equipment are earning well above their cost of capital. However, cost of sales still rose to $870,000 alongside the 11.3% electricity price increase, and the co-op carries concentration risk on a few large e-commerce contracts; if the Sunday trial or evening slots underperform, margins could slip back.

Conclusion: BRD's financial performance has improved. Trading margins rose from 35.0% to 40.0%, operating returns from 10.0% to 12.0% and capital efficiency from 12.0% to 14.5%, on revenue growth of $250,000. The surplus position is healthy for a co-operative, but BRD should protect it by locking electricity tariffs, keeping labour turnover below 31% through rotation, and only converting member shares to permanent capital as surpluses allow.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost of sales, capital employed and interest movements and a justified conclusion on whether BRD has improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for BRD of offering same-day evening delivery slots for a $1 extra per parcel surcharge.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The $1 surcharge is exactly what the 66% of 420 surveyed shoppers said they would pay, so BRD can charge a premium that lifts contribution per parcel above the current $4.60 while filling otherwise idle evening van capacity after the day routes finish. It differentiates BRD from national carriers that only offer daytime windows, attracts e-commerce retailers chasing basket size, and strengthens the 38% growth in social media mentions that already feeds retailer enquiries — a direct route to higher revenue without new fixed costs before the vans arrive.

Disadvantage: Evening work risks overloading the 40-member courier crew that already shows 31% labour turnover and 8% absence, and may force BRD to pay unsocial-hours premiums that eat the $1 gain before it reaches the surplus. If demand is patchy, vans run half-empty and the surcharge story fails, and any missed evening windows — remember 92.5% next-day reliability has slipped from 95.0% — would damage the trusted green co-op reputation that partner retailers renew contracts on, undoing the premium pricing BRD is counting on.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to BRD's research, costs and turnover.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 4.75%, the 6.5% increase in the minimum wage to $11.61 and the 11.3% rise in electricity and charging costs will affect BRD. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 4.75%): The 0.5% increase on BRD's $320,000 variable-rate bank loan adds roughly $1,600 a year to financing costs, slightly lifting the pressure behind the rise in interest payable from $15,000 to $21,000 shown in 2025. It also raises the price of any future van finance. The impact is real but small, and the co-op can fix the loan or renegotiate at renewal, so it is the least threatening of the three changes.

Minimum wage increase (6.5%, to $11.61 from April 2027): BRD is labour-intensive — 40 member couriers whose pay is benchmark-linked to the minimum wage. The insert gives the new floor at $11.61 per hour, up $0.71 from $10.90, so every member paid at the minimum gains about $0.71 an hour and the payroll rises broadly across the workforce. The hours worked are not stated in the insert, so the exact annual addition cannot be quantified precisely — but it will recur every year against a $1.45 million revenue and $174,000 operating profit. It is partially recoverable through the $1 same-day surcharge and Sunday premiums, though it will also raise member expectations and affect morale either way.

Electricity and charging cost inflation (11.3%): Every delivery now runs on electric vans, so charging cost is a direct component of the $4.60 variable cost of each of the 58,000 parcels BRD produces. An 11.3% rise (with diesel only up 8.7% elsewhere) narrows BRD's electric advantage and erodes contribution on every parcel. The insert does not decompose the variable cost, so the exact annual impact cannot be quantified precisely; for illustration only, an 11.3% rise on a $1.00 per-parcel electricity element would add $0.113 per parcel, or about $6,554 a year across 58,000 parcels — illustrative only. However, BRD's absolute energy spend is smaller than its payroll, so the cash impact is moderate, not crippling.

Conclusion: The 6.5% minimum wage increase will have the greatest impact. Payroll is the largest controllable cost in BRD's model, and a broad, recurring uplift across all 40 members would weigh heavily on the $174,000 operating profit unless surcharges and productivity offset it — a systemic challenge, unlike the small interest rise or the manageable electricity increase. BRD should renegotiate retailer rates, secure the $1 surcharge firmly, and build the rise into member pay planning before April 2027.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to BRD.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on BRD's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of BRD with a well-justified judgement that the minimum wage increase has the greatest impact.
